questions.explanation: Forest intercepts rainfall in the canopy, returns part of it to the air through evaporation, and slows water at the soil surface while its roots hold soil in place. Remove that cover and the same storm produces more runoff, a higher peak because the water arrives in a shorter time, and more sediment because there is less root reinforcement and no canopy to break the drop. Every link in that chain is physical rather than statistical, which is why a paired catchment can test it, and the algal blooms follow from the extra nutrient and sediment the faster runoff delivers. The tempting belief is that a catchment's response to rain is fixed, and the practical consequence is that deforestation is assessed only for its carbon and its habitat and never for the flood peak it produces ten kilometres downstream.
questions.hint: Canopy interception, infiltration and root-held soil are the three links to check.

questions.explanation: Two lags stack. Nitrate applied in spring travels through the soil and the groundwater to the river over weeks, and the river then carries it to the estuary, which can be days to weeks more. Once there it does two things: it fertilises an algal bloom, and when that bloom dies its decomposition consumes dissolved oxygen. The bloom has to grow first, so the oxygen demand arrives after the nitrogen, and warm summer water holds less oxygen to begin with, which is why the same load does far more damage in August than in April. The tempting belief is that a cause and its impact must be visible in the same week, and it is that expectation which makes a well-monitored programme look ineffective when the estuary record is simply being read on the wrong timescale.
questions.hint: Ask how long the nitrogen takes to arrive, and how long the bloom takes to grow.

questions.explanation: Every link in that chain is easy to state and only one is hard to measure. The price response is documented, and less combustion obviously means less of a given pollutant, so the fragile link is the attribution: a diesel retrofit, a change in freight routing or a shift in the weather can all move air quality in the same period. Attributing an air quality improvement to a price signal needs either a control group of unaffected road segments or a design that separates the two changes, and a simple before and after on the treated area cannot do it. The tempting belief is that the hard link is the behavioural one, because behaviour is invisible, whereas the confounding problem is not about visibility at all. The second temptation is to treat the whole chain as proven because each individual link is plausible, which is precisely the reasoning that a plausible chain has been mistaken for a measurement.

questions.explanation: A count is an estimate built on a method, and the method sets the detection probability: birds differ in behaviour, in season and in weather, so a count made at dawn, from a fixed distance, with and without playback gives a different number from one made at midday in wind. A difference between two sites is only interpretable if the detection probability is the same on both, and on a restored marsh with dense vegetation that is exactly what is not assured. The tempting belief is that a bigger count means more birds, which holds only when the detection probability is identical, and that is the assumption which makes most before and after wildlife comparisons fragile. The fix is a paired design with the same protocol, the same timing and ideally the same observer, plus an independent estimate of detection.

questions.explanation: A fall and recovery inside six hours is the wrong shape for most lake processes. Photosynthesis, temperature and loading all operate over days, and the closest thing to a six-hour event in a dissolved oxygen record is somebody standing next to the sensor with a calibration standard. The instrument log, the maintenance record and the raw calibration history are the first place to look, and only if the event survives that check does it become an environmental finding worth writing up. The tempting belief is that a sharp change must be a sharp cause, and it is a reasonable instinct on a smooth record and a dangerous one on a monitored one. The mirror-image error is to discard the reading as bad, which throws away a real event along with the artefact, so the correct outcome is a documented instrument event rather than a deletion or a headline.

questions.explanation: A species list records composition, which is one dimension of a wetland, and a restored system also needs the hydrology that delivers the water, the nutrient and carbon cycling, the disturbance regime that keeps the mosaic open, and the connections to the surrounding landscape. Replanting changes composition directly and the other three only indirectly and slowly, so a list of 40 species in a ditch that was drained and grazed is not the same as 40 species in a functioning wetland. This is why restoration monitoring has to include at least one process measure, such as water level, and preferably a reference site that was never degraded. The tempting belief is that the more species the better the restoration, which confuses a state variable with the processes that maintain it, and it is a convenient belief because counting plants is far cheaper than instrumenting a floodplain.

questions.explanation: A concentration limit constrains a ratio, not a mass, so the same mass in a smaller flow is a higher concentration and the same concentration in a larger flow is a higher mass. Settling at the upstream plant is a real reduction in what enters the water, but if the total was transferred to land or to a sludge store, or if the river's own flow fell, the measured concentration downstream can rise while the region's total load is unchanged or lower. A permit written on concentration therefore measures effort at one site rather than the quantity of material the river carries, which is why load, expressed as flow times concentration, has to appear alongside it. The tempting belief is that meeting a concentration permit must always reduce what a downstream user receives, and the correction is to compute the mass as well.

questions.explanation: Flooding a peatland releases the carbon that the saturated soils had been storing, sometimes enough to outweigh the ongoing uptake of carbon from the atmosphere for decades, and it also shifts the balance towards methane production, which has a much shorter atmospheric lifetime than carbon dioxide. Neither effect cancels the other and both belong inside the same carbon budget, over a time horizon that has to be stated, because a site can be a net sink in the long run and a net source in the first twenty years. The same structure applies to any land use change that moves carbon from a large slow pool into a fast one. The tempting belief is that a stored carbon is a protected carbon, and it is only protected while the pool is not disturbed, which is exactly the assumption that a reservoir on peat is built on.

questions.explanation: A bill is the product of two things, the amount of gas burned and the price paid, and only the first is an efficiency measure, so a billed total needs both a price correction and a weather normalisation before it means anything. The design that would support the claim is a pair of similar hospitals over the same two winters, one sealed and one not. The tempting belief is that a fall in a bill is self-evidently a saving, and it is the belief that makes almost every unmetered retrofit claim unfalsifiable.

questions.explanation: Runoff as a fraction of rainfall is 2.0 over 30, which is 0.0667 before clearing, and 4.0 over 30, which is 0.1333 after, so the runoff coefficient has doubled and so has the runoff depth for the same storm. questions.explanation: A concentration in milligrams per litre becomes a load only after the flow is included, and 15 mg per litre is 15 grams per cubic metre, so a flow of 2.0 cubic metres a second carries 30 grams a second. Working the other way gives the same figure: 2.0 cubic metres a second is 2000 litres a second, and 2000 litres times 15 mg per litre is 30 000 mg, which is 30 grams. The summer figure is worth carrying along as the check, since 0.5 cubic metres a second at 3 mg per litre is 1.5 grams a second and the two loads differ by a factor of twenty, of which five is the concentration and four is the flow. This is the correction that decides whether a rising load is being hidden by dilution or exaggerated by a low flow, and it is why a concentration on its own is not a measure of what reaches the boundary.

questions.explanation: An urban heat island is not a fixed offset, it is a nocturnal accumulation, and the two mechanisms that clear it are radiative cooling to a clear sky and convective mixing in wind. On a clear calm night the surfaces built up during the day lose heat by radiation with nothing to replace it, the built fabric releases the heat it stored, and the difference between city and countryside reaches its maximum, which is what the 3.2 degrees shows. On a windy cloudy night the same stored heat is mixed away and the contrast collapses to 0.4 degrees, and that collapse is itself the evidence for the mechanism rather than a contradiction of it. The design implication is that any heat island measurement programme must record wind and cloud, and must sample pre-dawn minima rather than daily means. The tempting belief is that a variable contrast means an unreliable instrument, when variation with a named condition is what identifies the mechanism.

Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen at saturation, so a lake at 25 degrees cannot hold what it held at 10 degrees, and at the same time a warm, nutrient-rich surface grows and dies more biomass, and decomposition of that biomass consumes oxygen in the water below. questions.explanation: The weak link is the one whose two ends are measured in different places, at different times and on different timescales, and that is the link from a river concentration to an estuary oxygen minimum, because the estuary integrates a different set of inputs over a different seasonal window. The links that are easiest to verify are the direct co-located ones, such as fertiliser application against the concentration measured in the tiles that received it, and a diagram that draws all four arrows with equal weight conceals that asymmetry. The tempting belief is that the strongest evidence sits at the ends, at the driver and the impact, because those are the quantities people care about, and in fact the intermediate chemical links are usually the best instrumented. Every arrow in a chain diagram is a hypothesis with a strength, and the diagram should say which.
questions.hint: Ask where each arrow's two ends are measured and on what timescale.
questions.learningObjective: read a driver chain and identify the weak link

options.misconception: assumes every arrow is documented simply because it is drawn
options.text: Nitrate concentration to the estuary oxygen minimum, since the two are measured in different places and seasons

options.misconception: treats a co-located pair as the best-evidenced link in a chain
options.text: Fertiliser application to nitrate concentration, since both are measured in the same basin

options.misconception: assumes that a field count is a better measurement than a chemical one
options.text: Oxygen minimum to flatfish population, since fish counts are the most robust field measure

options.misconception: picks the longest arrow in the chain as the best evidence
options.text: Fertiliser application to the flatfish population, since the chain ends in an ecological effect

questions.explanation: The budget is a set of pathways with measured magnitudes, and 300 kg entering the stream out of 800 applied is 37.5 percent, which makes the stream the largest single delivery route even though the crop removal is nearly as large. That is the number that matters for a downstream estuary, because the nitrogen that leaves in the crop has left the system while the nitrogen in the stream has not, so only one of the two arrows represents continued transport towards the impact. A budget is not required to sum to zero, since the arrows are measurements with uncertainties, and a residual term is usually present precisely because the terms do not close. The tempting belief is that the biggest term is the biggest problem, which confuses a sink with a pathway, and the other error is to read a permanent loss as automatically the important one.
questions.hint: Compare the magnitudes, then ask which arrows continue downstream.
questions.learningObjective: follow a nutrient budget diagram to the largest loss term

options.misconception: reads one arrow as the dominant pathway without comparing the others
options.text: The stream carries more than a third of the applied nitrogen, so the river is the largest single pathway

options.misconception: picks the largest term in a budget as though size implied importance
options.text: The crop removes most of the applied nitrogen, since 300 of 800 is the largest single removal

options.misconception: calls the smallest term the most important because it is irreversible
options.text: Denitrification at 200 kg is the most important loss, since it removes nitrogen permanently

options.misconception: expects mass conservation in a budget rather than a measured balance
options.text: The four terms must sum to zero, so the diagram is internally inconsistent

questions.explanation: The design subtracts whatever both sites saw from whatever the treated site saw, so a wet year, a price change and a regional policy all cancel because they are common to the two sites, and what remains is the change unique to the treated one. What it does not remove is a difference between the sites that was there before the treatment, which is why the before period exists and why random allocation matters: without it the two sites can differ in trend as well as in level, and a difference in trend is not removed by any amount of after-period measurement. The tempting belief is that adding a control removes every confound, and in practice a control removes only the shared ones. The design diagram is therefore also a statement of what still has to be measured, and the before period is not a formality but the only way to know the two sites were comparable.
questions.hint: Ask which differences the shared comparison removes, and which it leaves behind.
questions.learningObjective: read a design diagram and name the comparison it provides

options.misconception: assumes a control removes every possible confounded effect
options.text: Anything both sites experienced together, but not a change unique to the treated site alone

options.misconception: inverts the role of the shared comparison entirely
options.text: A change unique to the treated site, but not anything the two sites share

options.misconception: treats the control as extra data for one series rather than a comparison
options.text: The time trend in the treated site alone, with the control serving only to extend it

options.misconception: claims replication is provided by a design with no replication at all
options.text: Random variation within each site, once the design has been implemented

questions.explanation: The question is which two stations are as alike as possible except for the discharge, and B and D are the two tributaries of the same town, so they share the town's collection system, its treatment works and its storm drains while discharging to different water bodies. A difference between them cannot be explained by the town's discharge, because neither receives it. A and C bracket the town on the main river, which is the pair to use to measure the net effect of everything upstream, but the tributaries contribute a share of the load that never appears in that bracket, so the bracket is not a measure of the town's own contribution. The tempting belief is that upstream and downstream always isolate a source, and it fails whenever tributaries join between the two, which is most of the time in a real network.

questions.explanation: The diagram closes a loop in which the effect of more carbon dioxide reduces a removal process, and a reduced removal process leaves more carbon dioxide in the system, so the return path has the same sign as the initial change and the loop is positive. Its consequence is rate dependence: the system responds faster while the loop is running than it would have without it, which is why the size of the effect cannot be read from a single year's observations. The tempting belief is that anything that removes carbon is a brake, and a pump that is weakening is not a brake that is being applied harder, it is a brake being released. The mirror-image error is to call any self-reinforcing process a runaway, when the sign of the response to removing the driver is what distinguishes a strong feedback from a runaway one.
questions.hint: Ask whether the return path reinforces or opposes the original change.
questions.learningObjective: read a feedback loop and identify its sign

options.misconception: labels a self-reinforcing return path as a stabilising one
options.text: A negative feedback that slows accumulation, since the pump is already a natural brake on carbon

options.misconception: calls a self-reinforcing return path a stabilising mechanism
options.text: A positive feedback that speeds accumulation, since the weakened pump is itself a source of extra carbon

options.misconception: claims a partial negative response must be a complete one
options.text: A negative feedback that stops accumulation entirely within a few decades

options.misconception: assumes a self-reinforcing process must switch off when its driver does
options.text: A positive feedback that ends as soon as the carbon dioxide stops rising

questions.explanation: A load limit is a mass per day, so the measurement has to be on the line that carries the treated water to the receiving body, taken as a flow-weighted composite over a period that covers the diurnal cycle, because a grab sample can miss a release or a slug entirely. The bypass has to be measured as well, since whenever it is open the effluent is partly untreated and an effluent-only concentration then describes a smaller volume than the design flow. The inlet is useless for compliance, not because the treatment cannot release a pollutant, but because the concentration there is diluted differently and the flow has not yet been split. The tempting belief is that the treatment only removes material, which overlooks both a bypass and the mobilisation of a pollutant stored in the sludge, both of which are reasons a load at the inlet and a load at the effluent are not simply related.
questions.hint: Ask which line carries the water that reaches the receiver, and measure flow there too.
questions.learningObjective: read a process flow and identify where a measurement belongs

options.misconception: assumes a concentration measured at the inlet is a measure of the effluent
options.text: On the effluent line, because a load limit needs the concentration and the flow at the same point

options.misconception: assumes treatment cannot release the pollutant it was meant to remove
options.text: At the inlet, because the treatment only removes material and never adds any

options.misconception: samples one branch of the flow and calls it the plant's effluent
options.text: On the bypass line, because the bypass flow is the part that needs checking

options.misconception: samples a single point in a system and ignores the branch that carries untreated water
options.text: After secondary settling only, because earlier samples cannot affect the load limit
